questions.title: Question 1: Calls and returns (12 marks)
questions.prompt: A recursive method `power(x, y)` returns 1 when `y == 0` and `x * power(x, y - 1)` otherwise. Trace `power(2, 4)`. Show (a) every parameter value while the calls descend, (b) what each call is waiting to multiply, and (c) every expression and result while the returns unwind. State the answer and the number of calls. (12 marks)

steps.title: Read the question
steps.body: The command word is 'trace', so the answer is a table with the calls going down and the results coming back up. `x` stays 2 and `y` goes 4, 3, 2, 1, 0.

steps.title: Plan
steps.body: Write one row per call. Fill the Returned column going down (the expression with the recursive call unevaluated) and the Result column from the bottom up.

steps.title: Solution
steps.body: Going down: `power(2, 4)` waits for `2 * power(2, 3)`; `power(2, 3)` waits for `2 * power(2, 2)`; `power(2, 2)` waits for `2 * power(2, 1)`; `power(2, 1)` waits for `2 * power(2, 0)`; `power(2, 0)` is the base case and returns 1. Coming back: `power(2, 1)` = 2 * 1 = 2; `power(2, 2)` = 2 * 2 = 4; `power(2, 3)` = 2 * 4 = 8; `power(2, 4)` = 2 * 8 = 16.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: 2 to the 4 is 16. The calls are for `y` = 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0, so there are 5 calls: `y + 1`.

questions.answer: **Final answer.** `power(2, 4)` returns **16**, using **5 calls**. Marks: 4 for the descending calls, 4 for the waiting expressions, 4 for the unwinding results.

questions.title: Question 2: Diagnose termination (8 marks)
questions.prompt: For each method, identify the base case, the changing input, and whether the input gets closer to the base case. Say what happens for the input given and repair any method that does not terminate. (a) `static int a(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return n + a(n + 1); }` called as `a(3)`. (b) `static int c(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return c(n - 1) + c(n - 2); }` called as `c(1)`. (8 marks)

steps.title: Method (a)
steps.body: Base case `n == 0`. The input goes 3, 4, 5, ... so it moves away from 0 and `a(3)` ends in a `StackOverflowError`. Repair: call `a(n - 1)`. (4 marks)

steps.title: Method (b)
steps.body: Base case `n == 0` only. `c(1)` calls `c(0)` and `c(-1)`; `c(-1)` calls `c(-2)` and `c(-3)`, which go further below the base case, so it ends in a `StackOverflowError`. A method that calls itself with `n - 2` needs a second base case for 1. Repair: add `if (n == 1) return 1;`. (4 marks)

questions.answer: **Rule.** Every call must move towards a base case, and a method that reaches back by two positions needs two base cases.

questions.title: Question 3: The lecture's factorial (12 marks)
questions.prompt: The recursive method `factR(int n)` returns 1 when `n == 1` and `n * factR(n - 1)` otherwise; the iterative method `factL(int n)` starts `prod` at 1 and multiplies it by 1, 2, ..., `n`. (a) Do `factL` and `factR` give the same output for `n` from 1 to 5? (b) What do `factL(0)` and `factR(0)` do? (c) What happens if the base case of `factR` is commented out, and what is the cause? (12 marks)

steps.title: Part (a)
steps.body: Yes: 1, 2, 6, 24 and 120 from both. For valid input the iterative and recursive versions give the same output. (4 marks)

steps.title: Part (b)
steps.body: `factL(0)` returns 1, because the loop does not run and `prod` keeps its starting value. `factR(0)` goes to -1, -2 and so on and never meets `n == 1`, so it ends in a `StackOverflowError`. The base case does not cover every input that can reach the method. (4 marks)

steps.title: Part (c)
steps.body: Every call makes another call and none returns: infinite recursion. The frames fill the stack and Java throws a `StackOverflowError`. The cause is the missing base case; the repair is to put `if (n == 1) return 1;` back before the recursive call. (4 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answers.** (a) the same; (b) `factL(0)` is 1 and `factR(0)` overflows the stack; (c) infinite recursion from the missing base case.

questions.title: Question 4: Recursion against iteration (12 marks)
questions.prompt: Write recursive and iterative methods for the factorial of a positive `int`. Compare their output, the overhead of the calls, the memory used by the call stack, and readability. (12 marks)

steps.title: The methods
steps.body: Recursive: `static long factR(int n) { if (n == 1) { return 1; } return n * factR(n - 1); }`. Iterative: `static long factL(int n) { long prod = 1; for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) { prod = prod * i; } return prod; }`. (4 marks)

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body: Output: the same for every `n` from 1. Overhead: the recursion makes `n` method calls, the loop makes none. Stack: the recursion keeps `n` boxes on the stack at once; the loop uses a few variables. Readability: the recursion mirrors the definition `n! = n * (n-1)!`. (6 marks)

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: Every recursive solution has an iterative one and the reverse, so the choice is about when recursion is appropriate. Both overflow a `long` at 21. (2 marks)

questions.answer: **Rule.** Same result for valid input; the recursion costs a method call and a stack box for each level.

questions.title: Question 5: Convert a loop to recursion (10 marks)
questions.prompt: Convert the method `static int sumStep(int n) { int s = 0; for (int i = n; i > 0; i = i - 2) { s += i; } return s; }` to a recursive method with two parameters, and trace both for `n = 9`. (10 marks)

steps.title: Apply the rules
steps.body: The loop changes `i` and `s`, so both become parameters. The base case is the opposite of `i > 0`, which is `i <= 0`, and it returns `s`. The body and the update become the call `sumStepRec(i - 2, s + i)`. The first call is `sumStepRec(n, 0)`. (4 marks)

steps.title: The method
steps.body: `static int sumStepRec(int i, int s) { if (i <= 0) { return s; } return sumStepRec(i - 2, s + i); }`. (3 marks)

steps.title: Trace for 9
steps.body: `(9, 0)`, `(7, 9)`, `(5, 16)`, `(3, 21)`, `(1, 24)`, then `(-1, 25)` where `i <= 0` is true and the method returns 25. The loop adds 9, 7, 5, 3 and 1 to reach 25. (3 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** Both versions return **25** for `n = 9`; the base case is a range because `i` steps by 2 and can jump from 1 to -1.

questions.title: Question 6: Fibonacci (12 marks)
questions.prompt: The recursive `fibonacci(n)` returns `n` when `n` is 0 or 1 and `fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2)` otherwise. (a) State the value of `fibonacci(6)` and the number of calls it makes. (b) Why does it need two base cases? (c) Write an iterative method that displays the first `n` numbers of the series; for `n = 6` it displays `0 1 1 2 3 5`. (12 marks)

steps.title: Part (a)
steps.body: `fibonacci(6)` is 8. The calls form a tree: 25 calls in all, with `fibonacci(2)` called 5 times. (4 marks)

steps.title: Part (b)
steps.body: The recursive case reaches back to `n - 1` and `n - 2`. With only `fibonacci(0)` defined, `fibonacci(1)` would call `fibonacci(-1)`, which never reaches a base case. Both 0 and 1 must be answered directly. (4 marks)

steps.title: Part (c)
steps.body: `static void fibonacci(int n) { int a = 0; int b = 1; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { System.out.print(a + " "); int next = a + b; a = b; b = next; } System.out.println(); }`. For `n = 6` it prints `0 1 1 2 3 5`. (4 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answers.** (a) 8 and 25 calls; (b) the recursive case reaches back two positions; (c) the loop above.
